prompt.context: Office Vending Services Inc. (OVS) is the market leader in office vending machine services. The business services provided include sales and delivery of product, restocking of machines, and repair of faulty equipment. Profits are substantially down in the business.
prompt.question: The CEO of Office Vending Services needs Bain to assess the root causes of the profitability decline.

clarifying_info.q: What are the major cost buckets for a firm like OVS?
clarifying_info.a: Key cost categories include cost of goods sold (COGS), delivery costs, SG&A, and direct labor for repair.
Yes — exhibit data on revenue trends over 1996-1998 is available.

framework: Revenue analysis: Is OVS's revenue decline driven by volume, price, or mix? Examine trends across 1996-1998.
Cost analysis: Are costs declining fast enough to offset revenue decline? Identify major cost buckets (COGS, delivery, SG&A, repair) and trends.
Customer analysis: Are customer wants and needs being met? Assess importance vs. performance on key attributes.
Competitive analysis: How is OVS performing relative to competitors? Are there new entrants or share-takers? What are rivals doing better?

questions.prompt: What is happening to OVS revenues over 1996-1998? What is the rate of change?
questions.guidance: Revenues are declining and the rate of decline is accelerating. Down 8% from 1996-1997 ($250M to $230M); down 13% from 1997-1998 ($230M to $200M). Candidate should identify the accelerating decline and probe its drivers (volume vs. price).

math.answer: Revenue declined 8% then 13% year-over-year; rate of decline is increasing.

questions.prompt: What is happening to OVS costs over 1996-1998? Are costs keeping pace with revenue decline?
questions.guidance: Costs are also declining but at a slower rate than revenue. Down 4% from 1996-1997 ($225M to $216M); down ~7.5% from 1997-1998 ($216M to $200M). Cost reductions are not keeping pace with revenue decline, hence shrinking and eventually zero profit margin.

math.answer: Costs fell 4% then 7.5% YoY, lagging revenue declines of 8% and 13%. Profit collapsed from $25M to $0M.

questions.prompt: What is driving the revenue decline — volume or price?
questions.guidance: Volume (number of deliveries) has been declining while average price per delivery has remained stable. Therefore revenue decline is entirely volume-driven. Candidate should ask what is driving volume loss (market share loss).

steps: Exhibit 4 shows price per delivery flat across 1995-1998
Revenue = Price × Volume; since price is flat, revenue decline = volume decline
math.answer: Revenue decline is purely volume-driven; price has been stable.

questions.prompt: How is OVS performing in terms of market share?
questions.guidance: OVS has lost 20% market share over 1996-1998 while the total market grew 3%. Vend International grew 44%, Candy & Pop grew 22%. Candidate should calculate total market size and OVS's current share, and identify Vend International as the key threat.

math.setup: From Exhibit 5 (1998 figures): OVS $200M, Vend $130M, Candy $110M, Others $60M
steps: OVS lost 20% of its share 1996-1998 while Vend grew 44%
math.answer: OVS holds 40% share ($200M) but has lost 20% share; Vend International is the fastest-growing rival at +44%.

questions.prompt: What do customers care about, and how does OVS compare to competitors on those attributes?
questions.guidance: The top two attributes by customer importance are Price (10) and Delivery Reliability (9). OVS scores lowest on both (Price: 4, Delivery: 5). Vend International scores highest on both (Price: 10, Delivery: 10). OVS scores highest on Product Variety (9) and Machine Service/Repair (7), but these are the least important to customers (6 and 3). This explains why Vend is winning share: it meets customer needs where it counts.

questions.prompt: How do OVS's profit margins compare to competitors?
questions.guidance: OVS has zero profit margin (revenues equal costs). Vend and Candy are significantly more profitable. Candidate should calculate margins from Exhibit 8.

math.setup: From Exhibit 8 (1998): Revenue and total costs for each firm
math.answer: OVS margin = 0%; Vend margin ≈ 10%; Candy margin ≈ 11%. OVS is far less efficient than competitors.

questions.prompt: How does OVS's cost structure per delivery compare to competitors? Where are the differences?
questions.guidance: OVS cost per delivery ($105) is 9.5% higher than competitors (~$94-95). Within cost per delivery, COGS and SG&A make up ~70% of OVS's delivery cost vs. ~50% for competitors. OVS spends far less on the delivery labor/logistics component (~half of what competitors spend), even though delivery reliability is the #2 customer priority. This mismatch explains both higher costs and lower customer satisfaction.

steps: OVS COGS+SGA share of delivery cost: ~70%; competitors ~50%
OVS delivery bucket: ~half of competitors' delivery spend
math.answer: OVS cost per delivery is ~9.5% above competitors; overweight on COGS/SGA, underweight on delivery execution.

questions.prompt: Where have OVS's cost reductions come from historically? Are they cutting in the right places?
questions.guidance: OVS has reduced total costs 11% from 1996-1998, but the largest reduction has been in delivery (-25%), which is the most important attribute to customers. Reductions in COGS (-14%) and SG&A (-8%) have been more modest. This shows OVS is cutting costs in exactly the wrong place — degrading delivery while not sufficiently reducing product/overhead costs.

math.answer: Biggest cost cut was delivery (-25%), the very area customers value most; COGS cuts (-14%) lag behind the opportunity.

brainstorming.prompt: What specific actions could OVS take to reduce COGS and improve delivery performance?

categories.name: Reduce COGS via product rationalization
ideas: Reduce product variety/SKU count since variety is low-importance to customers
Purchase higher volumes of fewer products to gain economies of scale
Negotiate better supplier pricing with consolidated purchasing
Standardize machine-compatible product formats to reduce complexity

categories.name: Improve delivery performance and reliability
ideas: Optimize delivery routes using routing software
Increase delivery frequency to high-volume accounts
Reallocate savings from COGS/repair to delivery budget

categories.name: Reduce repair and SG&A costs
ideas: Reduce inventory complexity lowers order management costs in SG&A
Fewer product SKUs simplifies restocking and repair procedures
Outsource or reduce repair workforce if repair is less valued by customers
Automate reorder and invoicing processes to cut SG&A overhead

recommendation: OVS's profitability collapse (from $25M to $0M profit) is driven by volume loss due to unmet customer needs, particularly on Price and Delivery Reliability — the two most important attributes — while competitors (especially Vend International) excel on both.

OVS should realign its cost structure: reduce COGS by rationalizing product variety (enabling volume purchasing discounts), reduce repair spending (low customer priority), and reinvest savings into delivery capacity and reliability.
risks: Reducing product variety may disappoint some loyal customers who value selection; OVS should conduct further analysis on which SKUs to cut.
Improving delivery requires capital investment (drivers, vehicles, routing); payback timeline is uncertain.
Competitors may respond to OVS's improvements with their own price or service enhancements.
next_steps: Conduct SKU profitability analysis to identify candidates for elimination
Model unit economics of increased delivery spend vs. expected volume recovery
Benchmark delivery operations against Vend International to identify specific gaps
Assess pricing strategy — with lower COGS, explore whether passing savings to customers can recover price competitiveness score
